summary: Defines a new name form for the otherName field of the X.509 Subject Alternative Name and Issuer Alternative Name extensions so a certificate can be tied to an internationalized email address. It updates RFC 5280 and obsoletes RFC 8398.

plainLanguage.summary: An X.509 certificate can identify its owner by email address. The old name type for email, rfc822Name, allows only plain ASCII characters, so it cannot hold an internationalized email address. RFC 9598 adds a new name type, SmtpUTF8Mailbox, that stores such addresses, and it updates the rules for checking certificate names against domain limits.

questions: how to put an internationalized email address in a certificate
subtitle: How a certificate names an email address whose local part is not plain ASCII, and how to compare such names.

tldr.problem: X.509 certificates identify subjects by email address using the rfc822Name type, whose syntax allows only a subset of US-ASCII, so it cannot hold an internationalized email address.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9598 defines SmtpUTF8Mailbox, a new otherName form that stores the address as a UTF8String with the domain always in A-label form, and it extends rfc822Name name constraints to cover the new form.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 8398 and simplifies it by always using A-labels for domain labels. It also updates RFC 5280, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

today: RFC 9598 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 8398 and updates RFC 5280. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a New Name Form Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 5280 defines the rfc822Name name type for email addresses in X.509 certificates. Its syntax is restricted to a subset of US-ASCII characters, so it cannot represent internationalized email addresses as defined in RFC 6531. This document defines a new otherName variant for those addresses. It also requires all email address domains in X.509 certificates to conform to IDNA2008.

This document obsoletes RFC 8398. The primary motivation is to simplify the encoding of domain labels in the domain part of internationalized email addresses. RFC 8398 specified that domain labels are conditionally encoded using either A-labels or U-labels. This specification mandates the A-label representation in all cases, which makes encoding and processing simpler.
sections.plainLanguage: The old name type for email addresses in certificates accepts only plain ASCII letters, so it cannot hold addresses written in other scripts. This RFC adds a second name type for those addresses and requires one encoding for the domain part.

sections.title: The SmtpUTF8Mailbox Name Form
sections.content:
The GeneralName structure of RFC 5280 supports many name forms, including otherName for extensibility. This document specifies the SmtpUTF8Mailbox name form of otherName, so internationalized email addresses can appear in a certificate's subjectAltName, its issuerAltName, or anywhere else that GeneralName is used. Its identifier is id-on 9 and its value type is UTF8String (SIZE (1..MAX)).

The value follows the internationalized Mailbox syntax of RFC 6531, with refinements. Domain labels that include non-ASCII characters MUST be stored in A-label form rather than U-label form. Domain labels that use only ASCII characters SHALL use the NR-LDH restrictions from RFC 5890. All NR-LDH and A-label labels in the domain part SHALL be encoded with lowercase letters, so that two values can be compared octet for octet.

Like rfc822Name, SmtpUTF8Mailbox is an envelope Mailbox: it has no phrase before it, no comment after it, and it is not surrounded by angle brackets. The UTF8String encoding MUST NOT contain a Byte Order Mark, which keeps comparison consistent across implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The new name form holds one email address in a fixed encoding. The part before the at-sign may use any alphabet; the domain part is always written in a plain-ASCII code and in lowercase letters, so two certificates can be compared byte by byte.

sections.title: When to Use Which Name Form
sections.content:
For compatibility with legacy software and with name constraints, SmtpUTF8Mailbox in a subjectAltName MUST NOT be used unless the Local-part of the address contains non-ASCII characters. When the Local-part is ASCII, rfc822Name MUST be used instead, even when the domain contains Unicode. Legacy software that supports only rfc822Name therefore keeps working, and existing name constraints stay meaningful.

A non-ASCII Local-part may also include ASCII characters. Separately, all email address domains in X.509 certificates MUST conform to IDNA2008 and avoid the mappings mentioned in that document. This applies to SmtpUTF8Mailbox and rfc822Name everywhere they are used, because non-conforming domains would allow conversion errors between alternate forms.
sections.plainLanguage: If the part before the at-sign is plain ASCII, the certificate must use the old name form. The new form is reserved for addresses whose local part contains non-ASCII characters. The domain part must always follow one internationalized domain standard.

sections.title: Matching Addresses
sections.content:
Two SmtpUTF8Mailbox values are equivalent only if they match exactly, octet for octet, with no setup work. Comparing an SmtpUTF8Mailbox with an rfc822Name always fails: an SmtpUTF8Mailbox value always has a Local-part with at least one non-ASCII character, while an rfc822Name is all ASCII.

Comparing a certificate value with an email address from another source, such as a received message or user input, needs setup steps. First remove any phrases, comments and angle brackets. For the domain part, convert any U-labels to A-labels, then convert uppercase letters in the NR-LDH and A-label labels to lowercase. For the Local-part, verify that it conforms to RFC 6530 and RFC 6531 and is a UTF-8 string; it MUST NOT be transformed in any way, such as case folding or normalization. Then compare the strings octet for octet.

The specification defines no wildcard characters, and comparison implementations MUST NOT treat any character as a wildcard. To cover several email addresses, a certificate MUST list each one in its own subjectAltName or issuerAltName entry.
sections.plainLanguage: To check that two certificate names are the same, first put the domain part into the standard lowercase form, then compare the whole address byte by byte. The local part is never changed, so it has no special rules. There are no wildcards: one entry names one address.

sections.title: Name Constraints in Path Validation
sections.content:
This section updates Section 4.2.1.10 of RFC 5280 so that rfc822Name name constraints also apply to SmtpUTF8Mailbox names. Both forms represent the same email address namespace. RFC 9549 updates the rfc822Name name constraints so that a certification authority limited to certain domains stays limited when certificates use the new form. Name constraints that include a Local-part SHOULD NOT be used.

For a constraint check, run the setup steps of Section 5, then strip the Local-part and the at-sign from each name, which leaves just the domain. If the constraint domain starts with a period, a suffix of the subject alternative name domain, including that leading period, MUST match the constraint octet for octet. Otherwise the entire domain MUST match the constraint octet for octet.

Certification authorities that wish to issue CA certificates with email address name constraints MUST use rfc822Name subject alternative names only, with IDNA2008-conformant names and non-ASCII domains encoded in A-labels only.
sections.plainLanguage: A limited certificate authority may only vouch for addresses in certain domains. This update applies those domain limits to the new name form as well, so introducing the new form does not bypass an existing limit. The limit itself is checked on the domain part only.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Using SmtpUTF8Mailbox brings the same security considerations as Section 8 of RFC 5280, plus one new issue: non-ASCII characters are now allowed in the email address Local-part. Unicode introduces the risk of visually similar or identical characters that can be used to deceive the recipient.

A string of user-perceived characters can also be encoded in several ways in Unicode, and RFC 6531 does not mandate any normalization form for the Local-part. To limit attacks that exploit different encodings, this specification requires octet-for-octet comparison of the Local-part. The document notes that this binary comparison may raise interoperability concerns when the mail system uses one encoding and the certification authority uses another.
sections.plainLanguage: Letters from different alphabets can look identical, so a bad actor could try to pass off a look-alike address. Exact byte comparison limits that trick, but it can also reject addresses that only differ in how they were encoded.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 8398
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 8398 with three major changes. Domain labels in mail addresses are always encoded as LDH labels, using A-labels and never U-labels. The mail address matching algorithm accepts only domain labels in A-label form. The procedure for processing rfc822Name name constraints likewise accepts only A-label domain labels.

IANA has updated the references for the id-mod-lamps-eai-addresses-2016 module and for the SmtpUTF8Mailbox otherName in the PKIX registries to point to this document instead of RFC 8398.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier version allowed the domain part to be written in two ways. This version picks one encoding, A-labels, and updates the matching and constraint rules to match. The official registry entries now point here.
